The oldest komuz-type instruments go back to the fourth century; the archaeological evidence for the related Azerbaijani gopuz points to about 6000 BCE, and in the 1960s American archaeologists found clay tablets in Iranian Azerbaijan depicting a musician holding a similar instrument. Its range is comparatively narrow and sits mainly in the middle-high register, where it produces a clear, strongly penetrating sound. In playing, the tone feels light, and it is not as warm and rounded as a traditional wooden jaw harp. It resonates mainly by changing the shape of the mouth cavity to produce changes of pitch and timbre, and the sound carries a moderate nasal resonance. The temir komuz is the jaw harp of the Kyrgyz (Kirghiz). It has nothing to do with the three-string fretless lute, the komuz, in form or construction, and merely borrows its name. The instrument is made of iron, commonly about 100 to 200 mm long and 2 to 7 mm wide, and its range is mostly close to one octave. It is played by Kyrgyz children and by some adults, and has been played by national artists of the Kyrgyz Republic and in ensemble on the stage of the Bolshoi Theatre; in traditional Turkic music, Sakha / Yakut and Tuvan music also use it under similar names, and it was carried into Hungary by the Cumans. The Kyrgyz puppet theatre "tak-tek" uses it as accompaniment, the player plucking while pulling a wooden goat puppet with a cord in the right hand.
